summary: Describes SASL, a method for adding authentication to connection-based protocols. A protocol includes a command to choose an authentication mechanism, and may optionally set up a security layer. It was replaced by RFC 4422 and RFC 4752.

eli5.summary: It is a plug-in socket for logging in. A program can swap in different kinds of login methods without changing the rest of its rules.

questions: what is a sasl security layer
subtitle: A plug-in framework that lets any connection-based protocol add pluggable login methods and an optional security layer.

tldr.problem: Each connection-based protocol would otherwise need its own way to identify and authenticate users, and its own way to protect the traffic afterwards.
tldr.mechanism: A protocol adds one command that names a SASL mechanism. The client and server then trade mechanism-specific challenges and responses, and may agree on a security layer that wraps all later data.
tldr.outcome: Many mechanisms can be registered with IANA and reused by any protocol that follows the profiling rules. RFC 2222 has been replaced by RFC 4422 and RFC 4752.

today: RFC 2222 is obsoleted by RFC 4422 and RFC 4752, and was updated by RFC 2444. Use the newer documents for the current SASL specification.

sections.title: How SASL Works
sections.content:
The Simple Authentication and Security Layer (SASL) adds authentication to connection-based protocols. A protocol includes a command that identifies and authenticates a user to a server and can optionally negotiate protection of what follows.

The command has a required argument naming a mechanism. Mechanism names are 1 to 20 characters of upper-case letters, digits, hyphens and underscores, and must be registered with IANA. If the server supports the mechanism, it starts a series of challenges and responses defined by that mechanism as binary tokens of arbitrary length. The protocol's profile decides how those tokens are encoded on the wire.

During the exchange the mechanism authenticates the client, sends an authorization identity (often a userid) and may negotiate a security layer. The authorization identity can differ from the identity in the client's credentials, so a proxy server can use its own credentials but ask for the access rights of the user it acts for. An empty authorization identity tells the server to derive it from the credentials.

Once a security layer is agreed, it applies to all later data. Each buffer of cipher-text is sent with a four-octet length in network byte order in front of it, and may not exceed the maximum size the other side defined or negotiated.
sections.eli5: You tell the guard which kind of ID you will show. You and the guard then go back and forth until he is satisfied, and you can also agree to speak in a secret code from then on.

sections.title: What a Protocol Must Define
sections.content:
SASL is a framework, so each protocol that uses it supplies a profile. The profile must give:

  • a service name from the IANA registry of service elements for the GSSAPI host-based service name form
  • a command to start the exchange, taking the mechanism name as a parameter (and SHOULD offer an optional initial response)
  • how challenges and responses are encoded, how the server signals success or failure, how the client aborts, and how line length limits interact
  • the octet at which any security layer takes effect in each direction
  • how the authorization identity is interpreted
sections.eli5: SASL gives the rules for the lock, but each room still has to say where the lock goes and how to tell the guard which one you chose.

sections.title: Special Cases in the Exchange
sections.content:
If a mechanism has the client speak first and the profile allows an initial response in the command, that parameter SHOULD be used. Otherwise the server sends an empty challenge, and the client's reply serves as the initial response.

Some mechanisms send extra data from the server along with success, for example to authenticate the server to the client. If the profile does not allow that, the server sends the data as a challenge, the client answers with no data, and then the server reports success.

Unless the profile says otherwise, only one successful SASL negotiation may happen in a session. If multiple are allowed, there is never more than one security layer at a time. A later negotiation that selects no layer leaves the old one in place, and one that selects a layer replaces the old one.
sections.eli5: Sometimes the visitor speaks first, and sometimes the guard does. The rules say what to do either way, and you only get to show your ID once per visit.

sections.title: Registering Mechanisms
sections.content:
A mechanism is registered by filling in a template and sending it to IANA. IANA may reject obviously bogus registrations but does no review of the claims made. There is no naming convention beyond the syntax. Authors are encouraged to seek community review, and mechanisms meant for widespread use should be standardized through the normal IETF process.

The template asks for the mechanism name, security considerations, an optional published specification, a contact, the intended usage (COMMON, LIMITED USE or OBSOLETE) and the change controller. Registrations may not be deleted; a mechanism that is no longer appropriate is marked OBSOLETE. The IESG owns all mechanisms on the IETF standards track.
sections.eli5: Anyone can put a new lock design in the public catalog by filling out a form. Old designs are never torn out, only marked as outdated.

sections.title: The Four Defined Mechanisms
sections.content:
The RFC defines four mechanisms:

  • KERBEROS_V4: the server sends a random 32-bit number, the client replies with a Kerberos ticket and authenticator, and the two sides prove themselves with encrypted data that also carries the security layer choice and buffer size. Layers are 1 (none), 2 (integrity) and 4 (privacy).
  • GSSAPI: client and server loop through the GSSAPI security context calls, then exchange a wrapped 4-octet message carrying a layer bit-mask, maximum buffer size and, from the client, the authorization identity. It uses the same layer values 1, 2 and 4.
  • SKEY: the client sends the authorization identity, the server answers with a sequence number and seed, and the client returns a one-time password. It provides no security layers.
  • EXTERNAL: the client sends an authorization identity and the server decides using information outside SASL, such as IPsec or TLS.

Bit-masks that are not understood must be negotiated off.
sections.eli5: The RFC ships four locks to start: one using a trusted ticket office, one using a general security toolkit, one using a password that works only once, and one that just trusts the building's front door.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Choosing a security layer with at least integrity protection guards against an attacker hijacking the connection and tricking both sides into plaintext. The negotiation of the layer and identity is itself integrity protected.

The mechanism name is sent in the clear, and an active attacker can change which mechanisms the client sees. So a client or server supporting mechanisms of different strength should have a configurable minimum, and the check cannot live only on the server. New mechanisms must not let an attacker get weaker security by editing the mechanism name or the exchange. Anything negotiated before authentication happens in the clear, so it should be ignored or revalidated afterwards.
sections.eli5: A sneaky person in the middle might try to talk both sides into using the weakest lock. So each side should decide ahead of time the weakest lock it will accept.

items.label: Privacy
items.desc: Data is protected against tampering and eavesdropping.
